name: maturin
license: Apache 2.0 or MIT, at your option
summary: The build tool that turns a Rust crate with PyO3, CFFI or UniFFI bindings, or a plain Rust binary, into Python wheels, installs it into a virtualenv while you develop, and serves as a PEP 517 build backend.
intro: maturin reads `Cargo.toml` and `pyproject.toml`, runs Cargo, and packages the result as a wheel tagged for the right interpreter, OS and CPU. It picks the binding style from the crate: `pyo3` for extension modules, `cffi` (with a C header generated by cbindgen), `uniffi`, which generates `ctypes` bindings from an interface definition, or `bin`, which installs a Rust executable as a script on the user’s `PATH`. The distribution name comes from `[package]` in `Cargo.toml`, the import name from `[lib]`, and metadata in `pyproject.toml` takes precedence over Cargo’s. Three commands cover the loop: `maturin new` scaffolds a project, `maturin develop` compiles a debug build and installs it into the active virtualenv, and `maturin build --release` writes wheels to `target/wheels`. Because it is also a PEP 517 backend (`build-backend = "maturin"`), `pip install .` builds the same way, and a mixed layout keeps Python sources and the compiled module in one package.

Most of its work is portability. A Linux wheel may only link a small set of system libraries, the manylinux rules, so maturin checks the built library with its own reimplementation of auditwheel and tags the wheel to match. For compliant wheels you build in its manylinux2014-based Docker image or pass `--zig`, which links with `zig cc` for the chosen manylinux version; Rust itself needs glibc 2.17, so manylinux2014 is the oldest usable target. It cross-compiles to Windows MSVC through cargo-xwin, builds `abi3` and `abi3t` stable-ABI wheels with PyO3, and `maturin generate-ci github` writes a GitHub Actions workflow that builds wheels for Linux, musllinux, Windows and macOS plus a source distribution. maturin 1.15 builds for Python 3.8 and newer on Windows, Linux, macOS and FreeBSD. orjson, Polars, pydantic-core and Ruff are among the projects built with it.
strengths: From a Cargo crate to an installable wheel with no `setup.py`: package metadata comes from `Cargo.toml` and `pyproject.toml`
A short edit loop: `maturin develop` rebuilds into the current virtualenv, and PEP 660 editable installs work with mixed Rust and Python projects
Portable Linux wheels out of the box: built-in manylinux checks, a ready Docker image and cross-linking with zig
One tool for PyO3, CFFI and UniFFI bindings and for shipping plain Rust command-line tools through PyPI
limits: Built around Cargo and its own conventions; projects adding Rust to an existing `setup.py` package that can’t fit them are pointed to setuptools-rust
`maturin develop` is quicker but doesn’t support every feature that `maturin build` followed by `pip install` does
Builds through the PEP 517 backend are always release builds, so `pip install .` from source pays for a full optimised compile
Wheels are per platform: users on a platform without one fall back to the source distribution and need a Rust toolchain
Its own `upload` and `publish` commands are deprecated since 1.11, with `upload` due to be removed in 2.0; the README recommends `uv publish` instead

sections.title: What maturin can package
sections.intro: It detects the kind from `Cargo.toml`, or you pass `--bindings` (or `bindings` under `[tool.maturin]`).

items.name: pyo3
items.text: A CPython, PyPy or GraalPy extension module. Detected when `pyo3` is a dependency. With PyO3’s `abi3` or `abi3t` features one wheel covers many Python versions; otherwise each wheel targets one version, such as `cp314`.

items.name: cffi
items.text: A C-ABI library plus CFFI glue, compatible with every Python version including PyPy. maturin generates the C header with cbindgen and installs `cffi` into the virtualenv if it’s missing.

items.name: uniffi
items.text: Mozilla’s UniFFI generates `ctypes` bindings from an interface definition, so the same Rust library can also be bound to other languages.

items.name: bin
items.text: A Rust executable packaged into a wheel as a script, on the user’s `PATH` once installed. Detected when the crate has only a binary target and no `pyo3` dependency or `cdylib`.

sections.title: Getting wheels to users
body: `maturin build --release` builds for the machine it runs on. For Linux wheels that PyPI accepts, build inside the `ghcr.io/pyo3/maturin` image or with `--zig`, and pass `--compatibility pypi` to reject targets PyPI won’t take. Windows MSVC targets can be cross-compiled through cargo-xwin, whose use means accepting Microsoft’s license.

Most projects let CI do this. `maturin generate-ci github > .github/workflows/CI.yml` writes a workflow that uses the `PyO3/maturin-action` action to build wheels across Linux, musllinux, Windows and macOS runners, builds an sdist, attests the artifacts and, on a tag, uploads everything with `uv publish` using an API token. The guide also shows how to switch it to PyPI trusted publishing.

story: Packaging Rust for Python first meant setuptools-rust, a setuptools plugin configured from `setup.py`. On 22 August 2018 konstin released pyo3-pack 0.1.0, which described itself as “a zero configuration replacement for setuptools-rust”: it ran directly on a crate with no extra files, built wheels for Python 2.7 and 3.5+ on Windows, Linux and macOS, and could upload them to PyPI. Version 0.2 in September 2018 added CFFI bindings and the `develop` command.

With 0.7 on 30 August 2019 the project was renamed maturin, and the same release added PEP 517 support and the mixed Rust and Python layout, so `pip` could build a Rust package from source like any other. The releases after that went into portability and workflow: PEP 660 editable installs in 0.12.0 (November 2021), `zig cc` as a linker for cross-compiling and manylinux compliance in 0.12.7 (February 2022), and UniFFI bindings in 0.14 (November 2022). 1.0 followed on 23 May 2023.

Packaging around it kept moving. The generated CI workflow now publishes with `uv publish`, and maturin deprecated its own upload commands in 1.11 (January 2026), with `upload` slated for removal in 2.0. konstin and messense are listed as its authors.

choices.choice: Zero configuration on top of Cargo
choices.why: setuptools-rust needed a `setup.py` describing the Rust extension. pyo3-pack ran on the crate itself, taking the package name from `[package]` and the module name from `[lib]`, with no extra files to write.

choices.choice: Be a PEP 517 build backend, not only a CLI
choices.why: When pip finds no matching wheel it builds from the source distribution. As a backend, maturin lets `pip install` compile a Rust package like any other, from an sdist that contains the same files as `cargo package`.

Linux wheels that link libraries outside the manylinux set fail on other distributions. maturin reimplements auditwheel’s check, so it can give each wheel the right platform tag, or fall back to a plain `linux` tag, without a separate step.

choices.choice: Ship Rust binaries through PyPI too
choices.why: Packaging binaries arrived early, in 0.3. A `bin` wheel puts a Rust executable on `PATH` through pip, which is how Python users can install Rust command-line tools without Cargo.

timeline.text: pyo3-pack 0.1.0 released on 22 August; CFFI and `develop` added in September
0.7.0 on 30 August renames the project maturin and adds PEP 517 support
`zig cc` linking (0.12.7, February) and UniFFI bindings (0.14, November)
